title: National Nutritional Foods Association v. FDA
lead: After a massive hearing, the Food and Drug Administration standardized dietary supplements and restricted related claims. The court sustained broad regulatory authority while requiring meaningful exceptions, striking unsupported restrictions, and reopening a narrow part of the record for necessary cross-examination.

actors.name: Food and Drug Administration
actors.role: Agency adopting supplement identity and labeling rules

National Health Federation and Dr. Miles Robinson

proceedings: Following proposals beginning in 1962 and over twenty-two months of hearings, the FDA adopted final rules in 1973. The Second Circuit granted fifteen review petitions in part and denied them in part on August 15, 1974, stayed enforcement on specified terms, and remanded without costs.
limits: The court did not invalidate the entire program, guarantee unrestricted cross-examination, or approve every claimed exception. The later Kennedy litigation and subsequent legislative amendment were separate stages.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A diverse supplement market led to a vast formal proceeding
sections.cue: Introduce the program and statutory authority.
paragraphs: The Food and Drug Administration, or FDA, began proposing vitamin and mineral supplement regulation in June 1962. Objections to revised proposals prompted an evidentiary hearing under section 701(e) of the governing food-and-drug statute. More than twenty-two months produced 32,405 transcript pages and hundreds of exhibits. Proposed findings and tentative rules followed in January 1973, with another round of exceptions before final publication on August 2, 1973 and planned full implementation January 1, 1975.

Section 401 authorized reasonable food identity standards promoting honesty and fair dealing; section 403(j) authorized information disclosing value for special dietary uses. Part 80 standardized permitted combinations—all vitamins and minerals, all vitamins, all minerals, or vitamins and iron—and single nutrients. It specified mandatory and optional ingredients, names, and minimum and maximum quantities for designated groups. United States Recommended Daily Allowances derived from National Academy of Sciences recommendations replaced earlier minimum-daily-requirement labeling. Some conventional, restored, and low-dose products not represented as supplements were exempt.

Part 125 added dietary-use labeling but also substantive prohibitions. Section 125.1(c) generally excluded certain essential nutrients without established allowances; section 125.1(h) classified above-maximum preparations as drugs. Other rules addressed therapeutic claims, ordinary diets, soil and processing, unnecessary ingredients, and purported superiority of natural vitamins.

sections.title: The court reviewed the integrated scheme
sections.cue: Explain jurisdiction before the substantive objections.
paragraphs: Fifteen petitions challenged the program. Some petitioners simultaneously disputed appellate jurisdiction over eight provisions because section 701(f) expressly covered regulations under sections 401 and 403(j), while other rules ordinarily went first to district court. Judge Friendly, joined by Judge Smith and designated District Judge Bartels, distinguished arguable statutory authority from ultimate validity: a colorable invocation of those sections supported review even if it failed on the merits.

Drug classification was closest. A freestanding interpretation of drug status ordinarily required district-court review, as separate prescription-vitamin rules had. Here it was integral to an arguably authorized program, and splitting the case would waste judicial resources. The court reviewed all tendered issues, applying this formal proceeding’s substantial-evidence standard to the integrated provision rather than ordinary informal-rule review.

sections.title: Consumer confusion supported broad identity standards
sections.cue: Give the authority ruling and its limits.
paragraphs: Petitioners argued identity standards and dietary labeling were exclusive alternatives, dietary supplement was a function rather than a common food name, and section 401 reached only economic adulteration, not wholesome products or harmless excess quantities. The court disagreed. Section 403(j) did not exclude standardized food, naming requirements allowed practical flexibility, and dietary supplement had become a market designation.

Substantial evidence showed bewildering ingredient and dosage variation, inability to identify nutritional needs, and formulations disconnected from those needs. Labels alone might not cure confusion. Quaker Oats, the precedent on food identity standards, allowed exclusion even of beneficial ingredients and protection against variable composition beyond simple dilution. Legislative examples involving cheapened jam or butter did not exhaust the statute. Balancing increased costs to sophisticated purchasers against ordinary consumers’ protection primarily belonged to the agency; narrow exemptions did not make broader regulation irrational.

The court reserved whether every total ban on separately sold nontoxic nutrients was authorized and whether an imitation-supplement label could avoid standards, an option nobody sought. It found constitutional objections insufficiently substantial for discussion.

sections.title: Real demand required a meaningful exceptions route
sections.cue: Explain the ordered balancing and enforcement pause.
paragraphs: Broad power did not justify an all-or-nothing approach to combinations and maxima. Vitamin B complex might be understandable without every vitamin; clearly labeled 500-milligram vitamin C might meet demand without appreciable confusion. The court did not approve either automatically, but required serious consideration. The existing exception mechanism neither assured balancing of lost choice against added confusion nor permitted increases in individual maxima.

The FDA had to broaden section 80.1(b)(4), accept higher-dosage applications, and consider meritorious requests before enforcement. Demand, significant expert support, effective warnings, and reliability of a particular allowance mattered. The agency could maintain a manageable standardized market and need not grant many exceptions. An avalanche effectively reopening everything might be denied without prejudice, but vitamin C and B-complex requests had to be considered.

To prevent disruptive relabeling or withdrawal before decisions, the court stayed the whole scheme until six months after judgment became final or June 30, 1975, whichever was later, with possible extensions.

sections.title: Two substantive restrictions lacked sufficient support
sections.cue: Distinguish missing allowances from therapeutic intent.
paragraphs: No established allowance did not itself justify excluding an acknowledged essential nutrient. The agency lacked adequate explanation and evidence for that extreme step while permitting separate sales of less valuable substances. The court enjoined section 125.1(c)’s restrictions on those nutrients in general food, as optional ingredients, and as separate supplements. Combinations remained for agency consideration, with specific attention to omitted ingredients, integrating additional essential nutrients pending allowances, and clarifying nonessential substances. An uncertain unexplained ban could not be meaningfully reviewed.

The blanket drug classification also failed. Counsel’s pharmacopoeia-listing rationale was post hoc and would classify lower-dose vitamins as drugs too, contrary to the program. The agency’s actual claim that high doses had no nutritional use misread evidence: some people, including women using oral contraceptives, needed more than general limits. Therapeutic intent controlled section 201(g)(1)(B). Objective evidence could expose a false nutritional claim, but lack of food value for most people did not itself prove therapeutic intent. Section 125.1(h) was invalidated. Properly labeled high-dose products could still be sold as over-the-counter drugs; the ruling did not make every vitamin a food.

sections.title: The maxima survived substantively but required a fuller record
sections.cue: Connect the allowance debate to the denied examination.
paragraphs: Allowance information and minimum quantities drew less opposition than maximum tablet strength, generally 150 percent of allowances with specified exceptions. Critics said population estimates were imperfect individual limits and not designed as consumption caps. The court distinguished tablet strength from ingestion: purchasers could take multiple tablets at extra cost, and exceptions could accommodate special products. Experts disagreed, but the agency could select the best available revisable measure. The maxima were substantively sustainable subject to a procedural defect.

This was formal rulemaking under Administrative Procedure Act section 556. Section 556(d) protected cross-examination necessary for full and true disclosure, not unlimited questioning. Controlling repetition after eighteen months was proper, but treating all nongovernmental participants as sharing interests was not. The National Health Federation opposed nearly the whole scheme; the American Medical Association generally supported it.

Dr. Sebrell, former chair of the committee producing the 1968 allowances, was a critical witness. Agency representations reasonably led participants to defer questions until his testimony. The FDA then declined to call him because he disagreed with some proposals. When the medical association called him, the examiner barred Federation representative Dr. Miles Robinson from cross-examining and denied an interlocutory appeal. Manufacturers focused on therapeutic products, and another consumer representative lacked Robinson’s scientific skills. Repetition could have been limited without total exclusion.

Sebrell uniquely supported important findings, yet effective questioning had not tested scientific process, uncertainties, bias, or intended use. The court could not exclude a significant probability that examination would change the decision or review record. Calling him as Robinson’s own witness was no substitute. It required reasonable cross-examination by Robinson or a similarly interested representative, using another qualified Board member if Sebrell was unavailable. This was a limited reopening, not an unrestricted new hearing, and exceptions work could continue.

sections.title: Most labeling limits remained, with an iron qualification
sections.cue: State the surviving restrictions and produce relief.
paragraphs: The court upheld informational labels and prohibitions on misleading therapeutic assertions, unsupported claims that soil or processing caused dietary deficiency, nutritionally unnecessary combination ingredients, and claims that identical vitamins were better merely because natural. Literally true statements could mislead, but supported specific nutrient claims, factual origins, and recognition of deficient unbalanced diets remained permissible. Loss from a particular food did not establish deficiency in an overall varied diet.

Iron required more work: strong uncontradicted evidence indicated that women of childbearing age and children could struggle to obtain enough from a balanced ordinary diet. The agency needed further evidence or a qualified prohibition.

Sunkist also secured an injunction against applying Parts 80 and 125 to natural fresh fruit and vegetables. Section 401’s produce provisos and natural nutritional variation limited the scheme; promotional nutritional statements did not erase those safeguards. Fortification creating a fabricated product differed, but no demonstrated intended practice required relief on that theory.

sections.title: The remaining procedural attacks did not undo the proceeding
paragraphs: The court rejected objections to hiring and assigning Examiner Harris while the only existing examiner was occupied and borrowing another agency’s examiner for this lengthy matter was impracticable. Publicly documented meetings concerned expedition, not demonstrated merits influence or prejudice. Written direct testimony, schedules, evidentiary decisions, and intemperate exchanges did not warrant reversal. Other curtailed cross-examinations lacked a sufficient showing of possible effect on the agency decision or judicial review.

On August 15, 1974, the unanimous court granted the petitions in part and denied them in part, ordered the specified stay and injunctions, and remanded without costs. Broad standards authority survived alongside required exceptions, targeted substantive corrections, and limited further examination.
